_note: Every entry is an open question. 'says' states what the document says (with clauses). 'unclear' states the gap. 'workingView' is our cautious practice until legal counsel confirms. All of this is interpretation.

items.title: When do the rules start, and what about content already live?
items.says: The cover notice says immediate effect. §1.2 says the date of publication by NMC.
items.unclear: There is no grace period, no rule on legacy content, and no definition of when “published” is met for ongoing content such as old blogs or old reels.
items.workingView: Treat live content as in scope from 06/10/2026 and fix it through the Fix-now register.

items.title: Does the guide apply to wellness and diagnostics clients that are not doctors or clinical establishments?
items.says: The Guidelines apply to RMPs and hospitals or medical institutions, defined in §3.4 and §3.7. “Other concerned stakeholders” are told to comply (cover notice).
items.unclear: Whether a wellness centre, a diagnostic lab or a med-spa without a doctor is in scope.
items.workingView: Treat them as in scope for caution, and ask counsel.

items.title: Does agency work count as “engaging a third party for marketing”?
items.says: §8.1(ii) says a doctor shall not engage any third party for marketing medical services. §8.1(viii) and §4.4 refer to engaging agencies and digital marketing agencies.
items.unclear: How these fit together. Read strictly, §8.1(ii) could affect all agency marketing. §4.4 and §8.1(viii) suggest agencies are expected to exist.
items.workingView: Assume agencies may work, within the limits, with documented client authorisation. Ask counsel.

items.title: Performance-based fees: is a “lead” the “procurement of individual patients”?
items.says: §8.1(viii) says agency payment must not be linked to the procurement or referral of individual patients. §8.1(vii) bars lead-generation fees connected with referral or procurement of patients.
items.unclear: Whether cost-per-lead, cost-per-click, a percentage of ad spend, or a fee per booked appointment is covered.
items.workingView: Treat fees tied to patient-level outcomes (per patient, per booking) as higher risk. Fixed retainers and ad-spend-based fees look lower risk. Needs legal advice.

items.title: Doctor photographs on websites, ads and social
items.says: §9.2 says use of a doctor's photograph is not permitted where it constitutes self-advertisement, solicitation or promotional publicity.
items.unclear: Where the line is. A bio photo, a hero banner, an ad creative and a social post may be treated differently.
items.workingView: Avoid doctor photos in ads and hero banners. A photo with a factual directory entry is lower risk.

items.title: Scope of the “scientific or educational” case exception
items.says: §8.1(v) bars cases, results and before-and-after except where published strictly for scientific or educational purposes with anonymised patient consent. §8.2(i) allows research-based communication of case studies published in reputed journals. §6.2 says consent does not make a prohibited practice permissible.
items.unclear: Whether a clinic can post an anonymised case on its own blog or social as education, what counts as a “reputed” journal, and how §6.2 interacts with the exception.
items.workingView: Allow only content that is a summary of a published journal article, linked to it, with no promotional framing. Everything else is removed.

items.title: Are AI promotional campaigns banned or allowed with a label?
items.says: §7.2 says an AI-generated promotional campaign for furtherance of commercial interest is prohibited, and that compliant AI-generated promotional content must carry an AI source mark.
items.unclear: The two statements conflict on their face. It is also unclear whether AI-assisted drafting, AI image editing or AI-generated stock images need the label.
items.workingView: Avoid AI-generated promotional campaigns. Label any AI-generated content in use. Keep humans in charge of the final text.

items.title: Reviews: passive display, replies and neutral feedback links
items.says: §3.2 Expl. V bars soliciting, purchasing, procuring or manipulating fake, paid or misleading reviews, and bars a doctor from requesting or sharing testimonials or reviews for promotion on social media. §8.1(xii) bars fake reviews and manipulation.
items.unclear: Whether genuine, unsolicited Google reviews may stay visible on GBP, whether a neutral feedback link is “soliciting”, whether a website widget or ad extension counts as “sharing”, and whether replies are permitted.
items.workingView: No review requests, widgets, ad extensions or review schema. Keep review replies generic. Do not delete genuine reviews on GBP.

items.title: Discounts, packages and “free consultation”
items.says: §8.1(x) bars discounts, limited-period offers, contests, coupons, gifts, cashbacks, referral benefits, free procedures and similar inducements in a way that is likely to encourage unnecessary care or amounts to solicitation. The closing line allows factual disclosure of charges and packages.
items.unclear: Whether every discount is banned or only those likely to encourage unnecessary care. Whether a free first consultation or a package price is affected.
items.workingView: No discounts or time-limited offers. State fees and packages factually. Take any “free” offer to Leadership.

items.title: Educational content versus promotional content
items.says: §3.2 Expl. I exempts non-promotional information without commercial intent. §5.1 allows educational content that does not promote personal practice, solicit patients, or is monetised through promotional marketing.
items.unclear: Where the line is for a clinic's own blog with a booking button, or for paid promotion of educational posts.
items.workingView: Keep educational content. Remove claims and heavy sales calls to action. Be careful about paying to boost education posts as appointment drivers.

items.title: Where must doctor identity details appear?
items.says: §3.2 Expl. III and IV require doctors and clinics publishing electronic media posts to disclose name, qualifications, registration status and SMR/NMR number.
items.unclear: Whether this applies to every post and page or once per profile or site, and what counts as “transparent”.
items.workingView: Show it on the doctor profile, the footer, every blog byline and in social bios and posts featuring the doctor.

items.title: Superlatives and “years of experience”
items.says: §8.1(ix) allows superiority claims if objectively verifiable, with an independently ascertainable methodology. §8.1(iii) bars personal achievements and unverifiable claims, and names patient counts and success rates.
items.unclear: Whether “years of experience”, “senior consultant”, “experienced” and qualifications-based descriptions are achievements, and what a workable methodology for “leading” looks like.
items.workingView: Allow experience only as a verifiable fact. Treat all comparative words as banned unless Leadership approves proof.

items.title: SEO, keywords and search behaviour
items.says: §3.2 includes search-engine promotional communication. §8.1(xii) bars manipulating search rankings, visibility or algorithms to create a misleading impression of professional standing.
items.unclear: The document does not address keyword targeting, using “best” as a keyword, location pages, schema, link building or competitor keywords.
items.workingView: Keep SEO white-hat. Do not use restricted terms in our own titles and headings. Log specific questions for counsel.

items.title: Retargeting, custom audiences and personal data
items.says: §7.6 requires compliance with the IT Act 2000 and the DPDP Act 2023 and Rules 2025 to the extent applicable. §8.3(ii) says form, medium or frequency must not convert factual information into solicitation.
items.unclear: Whether remarketing and lookalike audiences built on website visits or health enquiries are allowed, and whether persistent targeting is solicitation.
items.workingView: Use audiences only with documented consent. Keep frequency low. Ask counsel.

items.title: Media features, “as seen in” and interviews
items.says: §3.5 names news articles intended for promotion and public interviews as media of advertisement. §8.2(iii) allows public-health talks in the doctor's own name and designation without promoting the employer.
items.unclear: Whether a genuine earned media feature may be displayed on the site, and how to tell it from paid editorial.
items.workingView: Do not buy editorial. Treat logos of media features as an awards-type claim that needs proof, and take it to Leadership.

items.title: Staff and clinic-culture content
items.says: §8.1(xi) bars using employees to promote professional services through prohibited testimonials, endorsements or recommendations.
items.unclear: Whether staff appearing in a behind-the-scenes reel or a team introduction is a prohibited endorsement.
items.workingView: Staff may appear in factual introductions. No staff recommending the clinic or its results.

items.title: Sponsored healthcare platforms and directories
items.says: §9.4 requires healthcare platforms to follow NMC norms, not to rank doctors for payment, and to keep listings transparent.
items.unclear: Whether a doctor who pays for a listing or a sponsored slot breaches the rules, and how to tell a paid slot from a paid ranking.
items.workingView: No paid ranking. A basic factual listing is fine.

items.title: Live surgery and procedure content
items.says: §7.5 refers to applicable NMC guidelines, directions or advisories on live surgery broadcasts.
items.unclear: The framework itself is not in the notice, so we cannot say what it requires or whether recorded procedure footage is covered.
items.workingView: No procedure footage for marketing until the client confirms the applicable framework and consent in writing.

items.title: Doctor's personal accounts and doctor-run channels
items.says: §3.2 Expl. III applies to doctors publishing electronic media posts. §4.4 puts responsibility on the doctor for content they authorise or knowingly permit.
items.unclear: How the rules apply to a doctor's personal posts that are not promotional, and to content we do not make but the doctor posts.
items.workingView: Share the Do and Don't summary with each doctor, and advise them to follow it on their own accounts.

items.title: State rules and later clarifications
items.says: §4.2 and §4.3 say statutes and State Clinical Establishments law prevail on a conflict. §12 lets NMC issue clarifications and SOPs. The notice is copied to State Medical Councils.
items.unclear: Whether State rules add requirements, and what clarifications will follow.
items.workingView: Check State rules per client. Leadership reviews NMC announcements monthly.
